## {.section-break background-image="../../sds-reveal/sds_frame.png" background-size="cover"}

# Conjugacy as a pattern

::: {.notes}
Block 1 — the framing move. Show that Week 2's Gaussian × Gaussian = Gaussian
wasn't a coincidence. When the prior and likelihood pair up a certain way, the
posterior stays in the prior's family. That's the whole point of this week.
:::

## The move we saw in Week 2

[Prior:]{.accent} $\mu \sim N(500, 20^2)$

[Likelihood:]{.accent} observation $D = 510$, known $\sigma = 30$

[Posterior:]{.accent} $\mu \mid D \sim N(503.3, 16.6^2)$

<br>

[**Notice:** prior is Gaussian → posterior is Gaussian. Same family.]{.yellow}

::: {.notes}
Quick recall. Spend 30s on this slide. The key observation isn't the numbers,
it's the closure property. If students groan, remind them: this is exactly
what we computed at the end of Week 2.
:::

## What "conjugate" means

A **prior family** $\mathcal{F}$ is **conjugate** to a **likelihood** $\ell$ when:

$$
p(\theta) \in \mathcal{F} \;\; \Longrightarrow \;\; p(\theta \mid D) \in \mathcal{F}
$$

<br>

[The posterior has the same functional form as the prior — just with updated parameters.]{.dim}

::: {.notes}
Slow down here. Two parts: (a) prior and posterior in the SAME family, (b)
"updated parameters" is the mechanical bit — we'll see the update rules next.
Conjugacy is closure under the Bayesian update operator.
:::

## Why conjugacy matters

| Property | Why you care |
|---|---|
| Closed-form posterior | No integration, no sampling |
| Sequential updates | Today's posterior = tomorrow's prior |
| Interpretable hyperparameters | Prior knowledge as "pseudo-observations" |
| Fast, exact | Good pedagogy + fast enough to compute on the fly |

::: {.notes}
This is the "why learn conjugacy at all?" slide. In Week 7 (Monte Carlo)
we'll see what you do when conjugacy fails. For now, when it works, it's the
cleanest tool in the box.
:::

## {.section-break background-image="../../sds-reveal/sds_frame.png" background-size="cover"}

# Beta-Binomial

::: {.notes}
Block 2 — the first new conjugate pair. Frame: we already saw Gaussian-
Gaussian. Now the same pattern for a totally different likelihood (Binomial).
:::

## Back to the bentos — but now with counts

Chibany's prior belief about tonkatsu rate:

[70% tonkatsu, 30% hamburger]{.accent} — but how confident?

<br>

This semester's data: **27 tonkatsu out of 40 bentos**.

[What's Chibany's updated belief about $p$?]{.yellow}

::: {.notes}
Story-frame. Last week we asked about the meal of a single bento. This week
we ask about the underlying RATE — which is a parameter, not an observation.
That shift (from meal to rate) is the conceptual payoff of this slide.
:::

## The Beta distribution

$$
\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) : \quad p(p \mid \alpha, \beta) \propto p^{\alpha - 1} (1-p)^{\beta - 1}
$$

| $\alpha, \beta$ | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| $\alpha = \beta = 1$ | Uniform on $[0,1]$ |
| $\alpha > \beta$ | Concentrated above $0.5$ |
| Large $\alpha + \beta$ | Narrow (confident) |
| Small $\alpha + \beta$ | Wide (uncertain) |

::: {.notes}
Intuition pump. Don't prove anything about the Beta yet — just plant the shape
intuition. The hyperparameters behave like "pseudo-counts of successes and
failures." That's the interpretation that will pay off in the posterior.
:::

## Beta-Binomial conjugate update

[Prior:]{.accent} $p \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$

[Likelihood:]{.accent} $k$ successes in $n$ trials $\sim$ Binomial$(n, p)$

[Posterior:]{.accent} $p \mid k \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + k, \; \beta + n - k)$

<br>

[**Just add the counts.** Successes bump $\alpha$, failures bump $\beta$.]{.yellow}

::: {.notes}
This is the cleanest conjugate-update rule in the course. Resist the urge to
derive it now (save ~10 min for the workout on the next slide). Emphasize the
interpretability: posterior hyperparameters are literal pseudo-counts. Frame
this as "the update rule is just addition."
:::

## Worked example — Chibany's semester

[Prior:]{.accent} $p \sim \text{Beta}(7, 3)$   ← encodes "70/30 with low confidence"

[Data:]{.accent} 27 tonkatsu in 40 ($k = 27$, $n = 40$)

[Posterior:]{.accent} $p \mid D \sim \text{Beta}(7 + 27, \; 3 + 13) = \text{Beta}(34, 16)$

<br>

[Posterior mean: $34/50 = 0.68$. Prior was $0.70$.]{.dim}

[Posterior is tighter: the data shrank the spread.]{.accent}

::: {.notes}
Play with the numbers. What if the prior were Beta(70, 30) instead of (7, 3)?
Then the 40 observations barely move the posterior. That's the prior-strength
lesson. What if we'd used Beta(1,1)? Then posterior is Beta(28, 14) ≈ 0.67 —
data dominates. This is the BIG intuition: priors act like pseudo-observations
and the data:prior ratio determines who wins.
:::

## Resume — Gaussian-Gaussian with N observations {data-menu-title="Gaussian-N agenda"}

Agenda so far: [Beta-Binomial ✓]{.dim}

[Now: what if Chibany weighs N bentos, not one?]{.accent}

::: {.notes}
2-min re-grounding after break. Surface the next conceptual move: from
one observation to many. Week 2 did one observation. Today we generalize.
:::

## Gaussian-Gaussian — N observations, known σ

[Prior:]{.accent} $\mu \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)$

[Data:]{.accent} $D_1, \ldots, D_N \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ (iid)

[Posterior:]{.accent} $\mu \mid D \sim N(\mu_N, \sigma_N^2)$ where

$$
\frac{1}{\sigma_N^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{N}{\sigma^2} \qquad
\mu_N = \sigma_N^2 \left( \frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{\sum_i D_i}{\sigma^2} \right)
$$

<br>

[**Precisions add.** N observations add N units of data precision.]{.yellow}

::: {.notes}
Same story as Week 2's single-observation case, but the "1/σ²" term on the
likelihood side becomes "N/σ²". Everything else — the closed form, the
precision-weighted average for μ_N — stays intact. Do NOT derive on the slide;
reference the Week 2 derivation and just generalize the answer.
:::

## Sequential updating — same rule, no new math

Observations arrive one at a time. Posterior after $k$ observations becomes
prior for observation $k+1$.

$$
\text{Beta}(34, 16) \xrightarrow[+1 \text{ hamb}]{\text{see 1 more}} \text{Beta}(34, 17)
$$

$$
N(503.3, 16.6^2) \xrightarrow[D = 498]{\text{see 1 more}} N(502.1, \ldots)
$$

<br>

[This is why conjugacy is useful in practice: online updates, no re-fit.]{.dim}

::: {.notes}
Forward-pointer to future weeks. In Week 7 we'll see what happens when you
CAN'T keep the posterior in the family — you have to sample. Today's happy
story is the exception, not the rule, but it's the one we can reason about
exactly.
:::

# Dirichlet-Multinomial (if time)

## More than two outcomes

What if Chibany has **three** meals: tonkatsu, hamburger, [curry]{.orange}?

[Prior on rates:]{.accent} $(p_1, p_2, p_3) \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3)$

[Data:]{.accent} counts $(k_1, k_2, k_3)$ from $n$ observations

[Posterior:]{.accent} Dirichlet$(\alpha_1 + k_1, \; \alpha_2 + k_2, \; \alpha_3 + k_3)$

<br>

[Same move as Beta-Binomial, with more categories.]{.yellow}

::: {.notes}
Stretch goal — cut if running short. The pattern generalizes: Dirichlet is
the multivariate Beta, Multinomial is the multivariate Binomial. Just add
the counts. Same rule.
:::

## Three conjugate pairs, one pattern

| Prior | Likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$ | Binomial$(n, p)$ | $\text{Beta}(\alpha + k, \beta + n - k)$ |
| $\text{Dirichlet}(\vec{\alpha})$ | Multinomial$(n, \vec{p})$ | $\text{Dirichlet}(\vec{\alpha} + \vec{k})$ |
| $N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)$ | $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ | $N(\mu_N, \sigma_N^2)$ |

::: {.notes}
Punchline table. The POINT of this week: conjugacy isn't one trick. It's
a recurring pattern. Mixture models (later weeks) and hierarchical Bayes
(Week 4) lean on these closed forms.
:::
